# 4g-usb-phone-mcp — Full Documentation

## Overview
MCP server that wraps the Huawei Balong HTTP API (E3372/E8372 USB LTE dongles).
Lets agents query signal strength, send/receive SMS, reboot the modem, and
manage network mode — all over the USB-connected modem's web interface.

## Architecture
```
Agent → FastMCP (stdio/SSE) → BalongClient → HTTP → Modem at 192.168.8.1
```

The BalongClient handles session token refresh (SesTokInfo) and transparent
retry. All state-changing requests go through the /api/webserver/SesTokInfo
auth flow automatically.

## Tools

### modem_phone (portmanteau)
| operation    | params                  | description |
|-------------|-------------------------|-------------|
| status      | —                       | Full modem status snapshot |
| signal      | —                       | RSRP, RSRQ, SINR, bars |
| sms_list    | —                       | Inbox messages |
| sms_send    | phone, message          | Send SMS |
| sms_delete  | sms_index               | Delete by index |
| reboot      | —                       | Power-cycle modem |
| net_mode    | net_mode                | Set auto/4g/3g/2g |

### show_modem_health_card
Rich Prefab UI card with signal bars, operator, network type, traffic counters.

## Configuration

### Env vars
| Variable       | Default        | Description |
|---------------|----------------|-------------|
| BALONG_HOST   | 192.168.8.1    | Modem LAN IP |
| BALONG_PORT   | 80             | HTTP port    |
| BALONG_TIMEOUT| 5              | Request timeout seconds |
| MCP_PORT      | —              | SSE mode port (omit = stdio) |

### Default modem IP
The Huawei E3372/E8372 defaults to 192.168.8.1 on the USB RNDIS/CDC ECM
network interface after plugging in. No configuration needed for basic use.

## Transports
- **stdio**: `uv run python -m four_g_phone_mcp.main` (Claude Desktop)
- **SSE**: `$env:MCP_PORT=11072; uv run python -m four_g_phone_mcp.main`

## Dependencies
- Python 3.12+
- fastmcp >= 3.4.2
- httpx >= 0.28
- prefab-ui >= 0.14.0

---

# Huawei Balong E3372 / E8372 — Technical Reference

## Identity

These are **4G LTE USB dongles** — data-only modems, not phones. No eSIM, no
Android, no voice/SIP stack. They enumerate as a USB network adapter (RNDIS on
Windows, CDC ECM on macOS/Linux) and expose a web UI at 192.168.8.1.

| Model | Chipset | LTE Category | Download | Upload | Antenna |
|-------|---------|-------------|----------|--------|---------|
| E3372h-153 | Balong Hi6220V100 | Cat4 | 150 Mbps | 50 Mbps | 2x TS9 external |
| E3372h-607 | Balong Hi6220V100 | Cat4 | 150 Mbps | 50 Mbps | 2x TS9 external |
| E3372s-151 | Balong Hi6920 | Cat4 | 150 Mbps | 50 Mbps | Internal only |
| E3372s-936 | Balong Hi6920 | Cat4 | 150 Mbps | 50 Mbps | Internal only |
| E8372h-153 | Balong Hi6220V100 | Cat4 | 150 Mbps | 50 Mbps | 2x TS9 external |
| E8372h-155 | Balong Hi6220V100 | Cat4 | 150 Mbps | 50 Mbps | 2x TS9 external |

## LTE Bands (typical, varies by SKU)
- **E3372h-153**: B1/B3/B7/B8/B20 (EU)
- **E3372h-607**: B1/B2/B3/B4/B5/B7/B8/B28 (Global)
- **E3372s-151**: B1/B3/B7/B8/B20 (EU)
- **E3372s-936**: B1/B3/B5/B7/B8/B20/B28/B40 (Asia-Pacific)
- **E8372h-153**: B1/B3/B7/B8/B20 (EU)
- **E8372h-155**: B1/B2/B3/B4/B5/B7/B8/B28 (Global/Americas)

Check SKU against local carrier bands before buying. B20 (800 MHz) is critical
for rural/indoor coverage in Europe.

## Speed (Cat4: 150/50)
Theoretical: 150 Mbps down, 50 Mbps up (2x2 MIMO, 64QAM). Real-world, with
good signal (RSRP > -90 dBm) expect **40–80 Mbps down, 10–25 Mbps up**.
That's fast enough for 4K streaming, video calls, large file transfers, and
as a primary connection for most tasks. LTE Cat4 is what most phones shipped
with in 2015–2018.

## Voice — None
These modems have **no voice/SIP telephony stack**. No circuit-switched voice,
no VoLTE, no analog audio out. They are pure packet-data modems. If you need
voice, you must run a VoIP app (SIP client, Discord, Mumble, etc.) over the
data connection. The 3.5mm jack on some models (E3372s-936) is for headset
SMS notification, not phone calls.

## eSIM — None
Physical nano-SIM only. No eUICC chip. No eSIM profile support.

## Walkie-Talkie / PTT Scenario

**Two modems on two notebooks = two IP connections to the internet.** They
do NOT talk directly to each other over LTE (carrier NAT blocks peer-to-peer).
For walkie-talkie / push-to-talk you need a rendezvous server:

```
Notebook A ──USB── Modem A ──LTE── Internet ──Server── Internet ──LTE── Modem B ──USB── Notebook B
```

Options:
- **Mumble** (self-hosted Murmur server) — lowest latency, true PTT
- **Discord** voice channels — instant setup, ~200ms latency
- **SIP VoIP** (Asterisk/Freeswitch) — full PBX, number dialling
- **Reticulum / MeshTastic** — not supported, these modems cannot form meshes

The walkie-talkie is an **app on the notebook** — the modem just provides
the data pipe. The MCP server here gives you signal strength readout so you
can position the modem for best reception before your call.

## SMS — Yes
The Balong HTTP API exposes full SMS control:
- **Send**: POST /api/sms/send-sms
- **List/Read**: POST /api/sms/sms-list (inbox, pageable)
- **Delete**: POST /api/sms/delete-sms
- **Storage**: ~50 messages on-modem

No MMS support in the stock firmware.

## Power
- **Bus powered**: USB 2.0/3.0, ~400 mA at 5V = ~2W
- **Peak draw**: ~800 mA during LTE transmit bursts
- **Thermal**: passive cooling, stays warm to the touch
- **USB extension cable recommended** in tight spaces (reduces RF interference from the PC)

## Connectivity

### How the computer sees it
When plugged in, the modem enumerates as:
1. A USB **network adapter** (RNDIS on Windows, CDC ECM on macOS/Linux)
2. A USB **virtual CD-ROM** (HiLink mode) containing the driver installer
3. A **virtual serial port** for AT commands

The OS gets a DHCP lease (typically 192.168.8.x) from the modem's built-in
DHCP server. The modem performs NAT to the LTE network.

### HiLink vs Stick Mode
| Mode | Known as | OS sees | IP | Use case |
|------|----------|---------|----|----------|
| HiLink | Router mode | Network adapter | 192.168.8.x | Default, plug-and-play |
| Stick mode | Modem-only | Serial port + NDIS | Carrier IP | Low latency, passthrough |

Stick mode requires flashing with a different firmware (e.g. "dashboardless"
firmware from 3G/4G resellers). The MCP server works in either mode — the
HTTP API is the same.

### AT Commands
Over the virtual serial port (CDC ACM / COM port):
- `AT+CSQ` — signal quality
- `AT+CREG?` — network registration
- `AT+CGATT=1` — attach to packet service
- `AT^SYSINFO` — system info
- `AT^NDISDUP=1,1,"apn"` — manual PDP context (stick mode)

## Antennas

| Variant | Connector | Gain |
|---------|-----------|------|
| E3372h / E8372h (with TS9 ports) | 2x TS9 female | Supports 2x2 MIMO |
| E3372s (no ports) | Internal PCB trace | ~1–2 dBi, omnidirectional |
| E3372h-153 | Comes with 2x small puck antennas | ~3 dBi each |
| High-gain upgrade | Aftermarket 6–10 dBi log-periodic | Massive improvement in fringe areas |

For permanent installations, mount the modem in a weather box near the window
with a **short USB extension** (2–3 m active USB 3.0 cable) and external
TS9 antennas.

## Where to Buy

| Source | Price (2026) | Notes |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| **AliExpress** | $25–40 | Search "Huawei E3372 4G dongle". Shipping 2–4 weeks. Check band SKU. |
| **Amazon** | $35–55 | Prime shipping. Amazon Warehouse deals ~$25. |
| **Local electronics** (MediaMarkt/Saturn/Conrad) | €40–60 | Buy local for easy returns. Often branded "HiLink" or "o2". |
| **Ebay used** | $10–20 | Second-hand enterprise surplus. May be carrier-locked. |
| **Refurb by Huawei** | $20–30 | Huawei's own refurb shop (sparse stock). |

### Carrier-lock warning
Many E3372/E8372 units sold by carriers (Vodafone, T-Mobile, o2, Three) are
**SIM-locked**. Unlock tools exist (`dfs -r` tool for Balong, paid unlock
codes from third parties, or Huawei's official unlock code generator using
IMEI). Some carriers will unlock for free after 6–12 months.

Before buying, confirm:
1. LTE bands match your carrier
2. Unit is **unlocked** or you have a way to unlock it
3. Firmware is "HiLink" (default) — avoids driver headaches on all OSes

## Firmware Flashing

### HiLink → Stick mode
Flashing converts the modem to act as a pure modem without routing/NAT.
This is a deterministic process using the `dfs` tool (Windows-only):

```powershell
# Download DFS tool and a dashboardless firmware
dfs -r e3372h_stick.bin --flash
```

Results in lower latency (~5 ms versus ~15 ms through NAT) and carrier-assigned
public/private IP on the USB interface. Trade-off: no web UI at 192.168.8.1.

### Unlocking
```powershell
dfs -r unlock /IMEI:123456789012345
# or use online Huawei unlock code calculator (IMEI → code)
AT^CARDLOCK="CODE"  # via serial AT command
```

## USB Interface Pinout (for reference)

```
USB-A male:
  Pin 1: VBUS (+5V)
  Pin 2: D-
  Pin 3: D+
  Pin 4: GND
```

The modem draws up to 800 mA. On USB 2.0 ports this is within spec. On some
older hubs, use a powered USB hub.

## Key Differences: E3372 vs E8372

| Feature | E3372 | E8372 |
|---------|-------|-------|
| Dimensions | ~90 x 30 x 14 mm | ~94 x 30 x 14 mm |
| Wi-Fi AP | No (E3372h/s) | **Yes** — 802.11 b/g/n, up to 32 clients |
| Antenna ports | TS9 on -h variants | TS9 on -h variants |
| Use case | Single PC | Hotspot for multiple devices |
| Price delta | base | +$10–15 |

The E8372 is essentially an E3372 with a built-in Wi-Fi access point. The
underlying modem chipset is identical. If you only connect one computer,
the E3372 is sufficient.

## OS Network Setup

### Windows 10/11
Plug and play. The modem installs as a "Remote NDIS Compatible Device" in
Network Adapters. DHCP gives you 192.168.8.x. The web UI is at 192.168.8.1.

### macOS
Plug and play (since macOS 10.11+). The modem shows as "Huawei Mobile" in
Network Settings, USB CDC ECM driver built-in.

### Linux
```
# The modem typically uses the cdc_ether or rndis_host kernel module
sudo modprobe rndis_host
# Interface shows up as ethX or enpXsY
# DHCP lease from 192.168.8.1
```

No additional drivers needed on modern kernels (5.4+).

## Performance Tuning

### Antenna Positioning
Signal quality is everything. The MCP server's `modem_phone(operation="signal")`
gives real-time RSRP/RSRQ/SINR. Walk around with the modem on a USB extension
cable while polling — aim for:
- **RSRP > -95 dBm** (3+ bars)
- **RSRQ > -10 dB** (low noise)
- **SINR > 15 dB** (clean signal)

### Band Locking
If your carrier has a preferred band, lock the modem:
```
modem_phone(operation="net_mode", net_mode="4g")
```

This prevents drops to 3G in fringe areas.

### USB Cable
Use a **shielded USB extension cable** (2–3 m max for USB 2.0). Keep the
modem away from the PC's PSU and monitor — electrical noise degrades the
LTE signal measurably. The MCP server's signal tool makes this easy to
verify empirically.

---

# Integration: 4g-usb-phone-mcp + telephony-mcp

**These two servers form a complete field-telecom stack.** One gives you the
cellular data pipe; the other gives you PSTN voice calls over it.

```
4g-usb-phone-mcp              telephony-mcp
┌────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Signal check        │        │ Place call with TTS  │
│ SMS send/receive    │───────▶│ via Asterisk/Twilio  │
│ Band lock / reboot  │  SIP   │ Call audit log       │
│ Traffic stats       │  trunk │ Contact management   │
└────────┬───────────┘        └──────────┬───────────┘
         │                               │
         ▼                               ▼
   USB E3372/E8372              Asterisk Docker
   (4G LTE connection)          (SIP trunk provider)
```

## Usage Scenarios

### 1. Remote Server Room / IoT Site (Primary Use Case)

A headless machine in a basement or remote site with the USB dongle as the
only internet connection. The agent stack provides both **connectivity insight**
and **alert escalation** in one loop:

```
1. modem_phone(operation="status")           # → signal 2/4 bars, operator "A1"
2. If signal < 2 bars: modem_phone(...,
        operation="net_mode", net_mode="4g") # → lock to 4G, prevent 3G fallback
3. In an emergency: call make_call(client=...,
        contact="Sandra", message="Server room temp critical")  # → PSTN alert
```

The agent never needs a separate internet connection to manage the modem or
make calls — both run over the same USB dongle's LTE link.

### 2. SMS Alert + Voice Escalation Ladder

Use the modem's SMS (free/cheap via bundled SIM plan) for routine alerts,
and escalate to voice PSTN calls (via telephony-mcp) if the SMS is not
acknowledged:

```
modem_phone(operation="sms_send",
    phone="+436641234567", message="Water sensor triggered")
# ... wait 5 minutes ...
modem_phone(operation="sms_list")  # check for "ACK" reply

# No ACK → escalate
from telephony_mcp.server import make_call  # via bridge/envelope
make_call(contact="Sandra", message="Water sensor - SMS not acknowledged")
```

### 3. Signal-Quality Gate for VoIP Calls

Before placing a PSTN call via telephony-mcp, check whether the LTE link
is stable enough:

```
status = modem_phone(operation="signal")
if status["data"]["rsrp_dbm"] > -105 and status["data"]["sinr_db"] > 10:
    make_call(...)  # good enough for VoIP
else:
    # SMS instead — more resilient at low signal
    modem_phone(operation="sms_send", phone="...", message="...")
```

This prevents expensive failed PSTN call attempts (€0.05–0.20 per call via
SIP trunk) when the signal is too poor.

### 4. Field Notebook Pair (Walkie-Talkie + PSTN Backup)

Two notebooks in the field, each with an E3372, running both servers:

| Notebook A | Notebook B |
|-----------|-----------|
| Mumble client for PTT | Mumble client for PTT |
| telephony-mcp for PSTN out | 4g-usb-phone-mcp for signal |

The 4G connection provides the Mumble voice channel (free). If Mumble is
unreliable (high latency, packet loss on LTE), telephony-mcp on either
notebook can fall back to PSTN calls — the SIP trunk runs over the same
4G data link:

```
1. Early in the field day: modem_phone(operation="status")
   → signal 4/4 bars → "good to go"
2. Mid-day Mumble degrades: modem_phone(operation="signal")
   → RSRP -108 dBm → "signal dropped"
3. Fall back: make_call(contact="Notebook B", message="Switch to phone")
```

### 5. Backup Link for the Fleet Dashboard (meta-mcp)

Register the USB modem as a network health data source in the fleet
dashboard. meta-mcp's `heartbeat_pulse` can probe both servers:

```
4g-usb-phone-mcp → GET /health → signal status → fleet dashboard KPI
telephony-mcp    → GET /health → asterisk/SIP trunk → fleet dashboard KPI
```

This gives the fleet a real-time view of "can we still reach the outside
world?" and "can we make calls?" as two separate health signals.

## Architecture Pattern: Agentic Dispatch Loop

```python
# Pseudocode — the agent decides this chain autonomously
status = modem_phone(operation="status")
if status["success"]:
    signal_ok = status["data"]["signal"]["bars"] >= 2
    if signal_ok and event_requires_voice:
        make_call(contact="Sandra", message=alert_text)
    elif signal_ok and event_requires_text:
        modem_phone(operation="sms_send", phone="...", message=alert_text)
    else:
        log("Signal too poor, cannot alert — queued for retry")
```

The USB modem provides both the transport and the signal-quality telemetry.
Telephony-mcp provides the voice application layer. Together they close the
loop: know your link quality, then use it.

---

# Future: sdr-mcp — The RF Layer

The third layer of the stack, below the modem's abstracted "signal: 3/4 bars,"
is **raw radio**. An SDR (Software-Defined Radio) lets you see, record, and
transmit the actual electromagnetic spectrum — the physical layer that the
Balong modem abstracts away.

### SDR is a Low-End Spectrometer

That's exactly what it is. Compare:

| | Lab SA (R&S FPH, Keysight) | RTL-SDR v4 | HackRF One |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Price** | $10,000–$50,000 | **$25** | **$300** |
| **Instant bandwidth** | Up to 8 GHz real-time | 3.2 MHz | 20 MHz |
| **Dynamic range** | >100 dB | ~50 dB | ~60 dB |
| **Calibration** | NIST-traceable | ±2 dB uncalibrated | ±2 dB uncalibrated |
| **Phase noise** | -120 dBc/Hz @ 10 kHz | -80 dBc/Hz | -90 dBc/Hz |
| **Stays plugged in** | In a cupboard, too expensive to deploy | **24/7 in your USB port** | **24/7 in your USB port** |
| **Reads by AI** | No ($50k instrument has no API) | **Yes, via MCP** | **Yes, via MCP** |

The tradeoff is **calibration vs access**. A lab SA costs as much as a car
and sits in a cupboard. An RTL-SDR costs as much as lunch and stays in the
USB port 24/7, feeding real-time spectrum into an agent loop.

When the modem says "RSRQ -14 dB" (noisy), the SDR is the instrument that
shows you **the noise floor**, **the interfering carrier**, and **the empty
band 3 MHz away** — exactly what you'd do with a field spectrometer but
readable by Claude.

> **Key insight**: A lab SA gives you certified power measurements. An SDR
> gives you _presence_ — "is this band clean or dirty?" — which is 90% of
> what you need for operational cellular work, at 0.2% of the cost.

## The Stack, Complete

```
Layer       Server              What it sees              Hardware
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Application telephony-mcp       Phone numbers, SIP trunks  Asterisk Docker
Data        4g-usb-phone-mcp    RSRP, SMS, LTE mode        Huawei E3372
RF          sdr-mcp             IQ samples, spectrograms   RTL-SDR / HackRF
```

Each layer answers a different question the LLM cannot answer from the layer
above alone:

| Question | Who can answer |
|----------|---------------|
| "Can I call Sandra?" | telephony-mcp (SIP trunk OK?) |
| "Is my signal good enough?" | 4g-usb-phone-mcp (RSRP, bars) |
| **"Why is my signal bad?"** | **sdr-mcp (interference? band congestion? wrong cell?)** |

The modem reports RSRP -115 dBm. You know it's bad. You don't know _why_.
The SDR shows you: "The cell your modem is camped on is saturated (high noise
floor on band 20). Switch to band 3."

## Hardware Tiers for sdr-mcp

| Device | Cost | TX | BW | Cellular use |
|--------|------|----|----|-------------|
| **RTL-SDR v4** | $25 | No | 3.2 MHz | Spectrum analysis, GSM decode (passive), LTE band scanner |
| **LimeSDR Mini** | $150 | Yes | 30 MHz | GSM BTS (private cell), LTE UE simulator, active probing |
| **HackRF One** | $300 | Yes | 20 MHz | Full duplex cellular experiments, signal injection, spectrum patrol |
| **ADALM-PLUTO** | $150 | Yes | 20 MHz | LTE UE, OFDM learning, carrier-grade experimentation |
| **USRP B210** | $1100 | Yes | 56 MHz | Lab-grade cellular test equipment, 2x2 MIMO LTE |


## Usage Scenarios: sdr-mcp + 4g-usb-phone-mcp

### 1. Spectrum Survey — "Why is my modem slow?"

The modem says RSRP -98 dBm (ok) but SINR 2 dB (terrible). The SDR answers
why:

```
sdr_scan(freq_start=800, freq_end=2700, bandwidth=3.2)
→ Spectrogram shows noise floor -95 dBm on band 20 (800 MHz)
→ One cell broadcasting at -72 dBm on band 3 (1800 MHz) — much cleaner

→ modem_phone(operation="net_mode", net_mode="4g")
→ But this alone might not switch bands...
→ sdr_band_force(cell_id="12345", band=3)  # future tool
```

Agents that can see both layers autonomously diagnose and fix RF problems
that would require a human with a field spectrometer today.

### 2. GSM Paging Capture — Silent SMS Trigger

An RTL-SDR running `gr-gsm` or `AirProbe` can decode GSM control channels
passively. An MCP tool could expose:

```
gsm_paging_sniff(duration_s=60)
→ IMSI 232-01-1234567890 paged on LAC 0x1A3B
→ SMS pending for subscriber
```

Combine with `4g-usb-phone-mcp` SMS tools: the SDR sees the network paging
the modem. The agent can then pre-fetch SMS via the API. Useful for RF
monitoring and lawful IMSI-catcher detection.

### 3. Cell Congestion Analysis

```
sdr_scan_lte_bands()
→ Band 20: 3 cells detected, load 78% (noise rise 6 dB)
→ Band 3:  2 cells detected, load 22%
→ Band 7:  1 cell detected, load 45%

Recommendation: Lock modem to Band 3 for best throughput.
```

### 4. Private GSM/LTE Cell (Transceiver SDR Required)

With a HackRF or LimeSDR and open-source cellular stacks (OsmoBTS for GSM,
OpenAirInterface or srsRAN for LTE), you can run a **private cell**:

```
srsran_start_enb(mcc="232", mnc="01", band=3, dl_earfcn=1650)
→ eNB started on 1805 MHz, 10 MHz bandwidth
→ PLMN 232-01 broadcast, 1 UE connected

# The E3372 can now camp on YOUR cell
modem_phone(operation="status")
→ operator: "sdr-mcp private" (PLMN 232-01)
→ signal: 4/4 bars (it's right next to the SDR)
→ WAN IP: 10.0.0.2 (routed through the SDR host)
```

This is an **entirely offline, self-contained cellular network** — no carrier
involvement. Useful for:
- Emergency response in disaster zones (no infrastructure needed)
- Secure comms where carrier networks are untrusted
- Lab testing of IoT devices without a SIM or carrier
- Rural/remote off-grid cellular

### 5. IMSI Catcher Detection

An SDR can passively detect suspicious cell towers (rogue BTS, IMSI catchers,
Stingrays) by comparing what the modem reports to what the SDR sees:

```
modem_cell = modem_phone(operation="status")["data"]["signal"]["cell_id"]
ambient_cells = sdr_scan_gsm(seconds=30)

for cell in ambient_cells:
    if cell.lac not in known_lacs:
        alert(f"Suspicious cell at +{cell.lac} — possible IMSI catcher")
```

### 6. Antenna Alignment (Field Ops)

Mount an SDR + directional antenna on a tripod. Sweep the horizon while
an LLM reads signal strength from the SDR:

```
for azimuth in range(0, 360, 10):
    servo_move(azimuth)
    power = sdr_measure_channel_power(freq=band3_center)
    log(f"{azimuth}°: {power} dBm")

→ Best bearing: 210° (azimuth with strongest signal, 12 dB above average)
```

Then check the result through the modem:
```
modem_phone(operation="signal")
→ RSRP improved from -115 to -92 dBm after alignment
```

## Forward-Looking: The AI Radio Operator

The long-term vision is an agent that operates all three layers autonomously:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              AI Radio Operator                │
│  (Claude / agent loop)                        │
│                                               │
│  sdr-mcp     4g-usb-phone-mcp  telephony-mcp │
│  ├ RF scan    ├ signal check   ├ place call   │
│  ├ spectrum   ├ SMS send       ├ log audit    │
│  ├ decode GSM ├ band lock      └ contacts     │
│  └ private BTS├ reboot                          │
│               └ traffic stats                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
  Physical LTE link ↔ Internet ↔ PSTN
```

Use cases this unlocks:

| Scenario | SDR does | Modem does | telephony-mcp does |
|----------|----------|------------|-------------------|
| Field site deploy | Scan bands, find clean spectrum | Lock to best band, connect | Report OK via voice call |
| Congested network | Identify least-loaded cell | Switch cells | Call quality test |
| No infrastructure | Run private LTE BTS (srsRAN) | Camp on private cell | SIP calls over local LTE |
| RF forensic | Capture IQ of suspicious event | Log modem state at that time | Alert via PSTN |
| Antenna install | Sweep bearing for peak signal | Verify RSRP improvement | — |

### Cost of the Full Stack

| Component | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Huawei E3372 (4G modem) | $35 |
| RTL-SDR v4 (receive only) | $25 |
| HackRF One / PlutoSDR (TX + RX) | $150–$300 |
| Total (receive only) | **$60** |
| Total (full duplex) | **$185–$335** |

For $60 you get an AI-controllable cellular stack that can:
- Monitor live LTE signal metrics
- Send and receive SMS
- See the full RF spectrum around the modem
- Diagnose congestion, interference, and cell load
- Detect IMSI catchers and rogue towers

For $300 you add the ability to:
- Run a fully private GSM/LTE cell
- Transmit on any frequency (within regulatory limits)
- Test MCP server responses over a real, self-contained cellular link

### Regulatory Note

Transmitting with SDR requires appropriate licensing (HAM radio license in
most jurisdictions for the 70cm/2m bands, or experimental/innovation license
for cellular bands). The receive-only path (RTL-SDR + E3372) has no regulatory
restrictions — you are allowed to look at spectrum. The moment you transmit
on cellular frequencies, you fall under telecom regulation. The agent should
check a jurisdiction config flag before allowing TX operations.
